lesson.title: How a Thought Becomes a Signal: The Basics of Neural Transmission
lesson.summary: Neural transmission is the process by which a neuron generates an electrical signal and passes it along its length and across synapses, forming the basic language the nervous system uses to communicate.
lesson.body:
A single neuron's job comes in two parts. First, it must carry a signal electrically within itself, from the dendrites that receive input, through the cell body, and down the length of the axon. Second, it must pass that signal chemically to the next neuron across the tiny gap of a synapse. Neural transmission is the umbrella term for this whole relay: electrical conduction inside one cell, followed by chemical transmission between cells, repeated across chains of neurons to move information through the nervous system.

The electrical portion starts when incoming signals at the dendrites are combined at the cell body. If that combined signal is strong enough, it launches an impulse that races down the axon toward the axon terminals. Many axons are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath with small gaps called nodes of Ranvier, and the impulse effectively jumps from node to node rather than crawling continuously along the membrane, a process called saltatory conduction that dramatically speeds up transmission, especially important for long axons such as those running from the spinal cord to the foot.

This electrical impulse follows the all-or-none principle: once triggered, it fires at full strength every time, or it does not fire at all, with nothing in between. There is no such thing as a weak or partial nerve impulse traveling down an axon. This means the nervous system cannot encode how intense a stimulus is by making individual impulses bigger or smaller, so instead it relies on how frequently a neuron fires, a firm pinch triggers a rapid burst of impulses, while a light touch triggers only occasional ones.

When the electrical impulse reaches the axon terminal, it must cross the physical gap separating one neuron from the next, since neurons do not directly touch. It does this by triggering the release of chemical neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft, which then bind to receptors on the next neuron. That binding can start a brand new electrical signal in the receiving neuron, and the whole cycle repeats. A signal traveling from the retina to the visual cortex, for example, passes through several such relays, electrical inside each neuron, chemical at each junction between them.

This combination of electrical and chemical signaling is what gives the nervous system both its speed and its flexibility. The electrical portion is extremely fast, impulses can travel at speeds up to roughly 100 meters per second along myelinated axons, but on its own a purely electrical system would be rigid. The chemical portion at each synapse allows signals to be strengthened, weakened, or blocked entirely depending on which neurotransmitters and receptors are involved, which is exactly what makes learning, mood, and the effects of drugs on the brain possible, topics this unit builds toward next.
